name: Perimeter
seoDesc: Perimeter: work out side length (b) (2) from the side length and the side length (a). A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: side length (b) (2) is what the Perimeter calculator works out, and it gets there from the side length and the side length (a). That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Perimeter calculator work?
sections.html:
The Perimeter calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports side length (b) (2) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the shape, the find perimeter given and the find perimeter given (2)); then you type in the side length (a), the side length (a) (2), the side length (a) (3) and the side length (c).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Perimeter calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Side length (b)=-side length (a) − side length (c) + triangle perimeter
Side length (b)=(1 ÷ 2) × triangle perimeter × (2 × side length (a) − triangle perimeter) ÷ (side length (a) × the cosine of (angle γ) + side length (a) − triangle perimeter)
Triangle perimeter=side length (a) × (the sine of (angle alpha) + the sine of (angle β) + the sine of (angle γ)) ÷ the sine of (angle alpha)
Angle γ=-angle alpha − angle β + 6283 ÷ 2000
Square perimeter=4 × side length (a)
Side length (b)=-side length (a) + (1 ÷ 2) × rectangle perimeter

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Shape set to Circle, Find perimeter given set to three sides (SSS), Side length (a) = 30 cm and Side length (c) = 30 cm. The calculator returns Side length (b) = -30 cm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Side length (b) = -30 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Shape set to Circle and Find perimeter given set to three sides (SSS).

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Perimeter calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the side length and the side length (a) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Perimeter calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns side length (b) (2), derived from the side length and the side length (a). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Perimeter calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the side length and the side length (a), which is 41 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side length (a) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side length (a) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Side length (b) = -30 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Perimeter calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
